title: Sugar Bowl

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of a Friend of the Museum, 1897
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A low, wide silver sugar bowl with a separate cover. It is decorated with flowers and combines silver with colored enamel.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, maker, date, medium, region, tags (Flowers), dimensions for body and cover, credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A silver sugar bowl with a separate cover, made around 1887 by Tiffany & Co., the New York firm. The Met lists silver, silver-gilt, enamel, and ivory as its materials and tags it Flowers. The bowl is small: about 3 5/8 inches (9.2 cm) high and 7 1/2 inches (19.1 cm) across overall.

descriptions.k: This is a small silver sugar bowl with a lid. Flowers are part of its design. It has some bright color in it, too. It is wider than it is tall. Can you find the flowers? What would you keep inside?
descriptions.g12: This sugar bowl was made in New York about one hundred and forty years ago. It is made of silver, with enamel, which is colored glass baked onto metal. Flowers decorate it. It has a lid. It is wider than it is tall. Find the flowers. What colors do you see?
descriptions.g35: Tiffany & Co. made this sugar bowl around 1887. It is silver, and the maker also used silver-gilt, enamel, and ivory. Enamel is powdered glass that is melted onto metal to add color. The Met tags the bowl with flowers. Look at the bowl and its separate cover. Why might a maker combine so many materials on a small sugar bowl?
descriptions.g68: In the 1880s, Tiffany & Co. made luxury silver that mixed materials and drew on nature and design traditions from around the world. This sugar bowl, around 1887, combines silver, silver-gilt (silver coated in gold), enamel, and ivory, and its flower decoration reflects a taste for natural motifs. At about 19 centimeters wide, it is small but rich in detail. How does the mix of metals and color change the way you look at a household object?
descriptions.g910: This sugar bowl of about 1887 shows how Tiffany & Co. turned a tea-table item into a showcase of materials: silver, silver-gilt, enamel, and ivory. The Met's subject tag, flowers, links it to the era's taste for natural motifs, while its low, wide form emphasizes surface, where decoration can be studied. Consider how color, metal, and texture compete for attention, and what the combination suggests about wealth and taste in the Gilded Age.
descriptions.g1112: Tiffany & Co.'s silver of the 1880s often fused techniques and motifs from multiple traditions, and this sugar bowl of about 1887 exemplifies that appetite for variety. Silver, silver-gilt, enamel, and ivory create contrasts of color and surface, and the floral tag in the Met record connects it to the period's fascination with natural subjects. The use of ivory also raises questions that museum visitors now ask about materials and the global trade behind luxury goods. Ask how the object negotiates beauty, technique, and the ethics of its materials.

teacherNote.context: Tiffany & Co. was a leading New York maker of luxury silver in the late 1800s. The Met record dates this sugar bowl to about 1887, lists silver, silver-gilt, enamel and ivory, and tags it Flowers.
directions: Have students design a small bowl decorated with a flower from their region and name the colors and materials they would use.
Ask students to explain how enamel is applied to metal and why it adds color that silver lacks.
Discuss why museums and the public now think carefully about materials such as ivory in older objects.
